# SK5040 — An XML resolver put back where the platform's default is none

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`XmlDocument` and `XmlTextReader` resolve nothing by default; assigning an `XmlUrlResolver` is a deliberate re-enable.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

A DTD can declare an entity whose value is a URI, and a reader with a resolver will go and fetch it — so a document the process was merely asked to parse can read any file that process can read and reach any host it can reach, and hand the contents back inside the parsed result or out through an error message. That is XXE, and it turns an XML endpoint into a file-read and a request-forgery primitive at once. What makes this decidable where `SK5009` needed two facts is that these two receivers have only one switch. `XmlDocument` — and `XmlDataDocument` under it — has an `XmlResolver` and no `DtdProcessing` at all. `XmlTextReader` has both, and its `DtdProcessing` defaults to `Parse`. On both, `XmlResolver` has defaulted to `null` since .NET Framework 4.5.2, so the safe configuration is the one you get by writing nothing, and an explicit `XmlUrlResolver` is somebody deliberately putting external resolution back. The defect is written out rather than inferred. ⚠ There is no fix, and the reason is `SK5009`'s rather than a weaker one: the mitigation is to leave the default, but this code went out of its way not to, so the edit removes a capability the author asked for. If the documents genuinely reference external entities the answer is `XmlSecureResolver` with a restricted permission set, not `null` — and which of the two applies is a question about the data, not about the code.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var document = new XmlDocument { XmlResolver = new XmlUrlResolver() };
document.LoadXml(untrusted);
```

Write:

```csharp
var document = new XmlDocument();
document.LoadXml(untrusted);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Measured unhosted, with a live control, and `CA3075`/`CA3077` are titled for exactly this gap.** On a plain `net10.0` project built outside this repository with empty `Directory.Build.props`/`.targets` above it and a `root = true` `.editorconfig`, under `AnalysisMode=All` with every `CA3xxx` and `CA5xxx` raised to `warning`, all four spellings produced **nothing**: the object-initialiser form, the post-construction `document.XmlResolver = …`, `XmlTextReader.XmlResolver`, and `XmlReaderSettings.XmlResolver`. ⚠ `CA3077` is `IsEnabledByDefault=True, DefaultSeverity=Hidden` in SDK `10.0.400`, so it is running silently in consumer builds already and still finds none of it. ⚠ **The zero is *shape present and declined*, not a dead run** — a planted `DataSet.ReadXml` in the same file fired `CA2351` and `CA5366` at the expected line, which is what separates this measurement from a build where the analyzers never loaded. ⚠ **`XmlReaderSettings` is deliberately excluded and this is the rule's boundary with `SK5009`.** Its `DtdProcessing` defaults to `Prohibit`, so a resolver on it alone fetches nothing and reporting it would report correct code; the pair of facts on that type is `SK5009`'s finding, and including it here would also double-report every one of them. ⚠ **Only a `new` of a resolver type, written at the assignment.** `null` is the safe value and is silence; a resolver assigned from a variable is silence, because whether that variable is null is a question about another method and following it is the inter-procedural analysis doc 08 puts out of scope; `XmlSecureResolver` is excluded by name because reporting it would be reporting the mitigation. This is `SK5009`'s value test, shared deliberately so that a resolver expression cannot mean one thing to one rule and something else to the other. ⚠ **An `XmlUrlResolver` carrying credentials is a finding rather than an exclusion, and issue #313 proposed the opposite.** Setting `Credentials` does not restrict *what* the resolver fetches — the document still names the target — it only decides what gets sent along, which makes a credentialed resolver a request-forgery primitive with the process's authority attached. `XmlSecureResolver` is the type that restricts, and it is the one excluded. ⚠ **The reference trees prove nothing here and the zero is reported as such**: the shape occurs zero times in either tree, and no file under `Testing/corpus` mentions `System.Security.Cryptography` either, so the corpus zero is *shape absent* rather than *correctly declined*. The measurement that decides this rule is its fixtures and `Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Tests/corpus/`, where every safe file is the same shape as its vulnerable twin with the vulnerability removed the way a reviewer would remove it.
